nodes.scenario: Kai is new to a friendship group where several people vape during breaks. Milo notices Kai has started joining them.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I didn't really want to try it, but everyone was outside vaping.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Did anyone actually ask you to take one?

checks.prompt: What is the most careful conclusion we can draw from the exchange so far?

options.label: We can describe what each speaker requested, while treating any account of their motives as provisional.
options.feedback: This keeps the distinction between what was said and why it may have been said. The latter requires more evidence.

options.label: We can take the last speaker’s explanation as the main cause, because it is the latest information.
options.feedback: Order of speaking does not determine evidential quality; the earlier words still matter.

options.label: We can give the two speakers’ interpretations equal weight, regardless of which one fits the details.
options.feedback: Plausible alternatives can receive different weights when the observed details support them differently.

options.label: We can infer that one speaker has a stable psychological trait if their response appears defensive.
options.feedback: A single interaction may reflect a situation rather than a trait that persists across settings.

options.label: We can stop analysing the situation because multiple explanations remain logically possible.
options.feedback: Uncertainty is a reason to test explanations, not to abandon reasoning.

checks.explanation: People can be sincere about their experience and still have incomplete explanations of why events happened. Social influence is not identical to coercion, and not all users begin through peer pressure. Nicotine dependence and health risks require separate attention.

nodes.title: Start with competing accounts

nodes.title: What should we find out?
nodes.prompt: Both interpretations are plausible. What would actually help choose between them?

glossary.definition: A belief about what people in a group commonly do or approve of.
glossary.example: A student thinks nearly everyone in a friendship group vapes.
glossary.limit: A perceived norm can be inaccurate, especially when noticeable behaviour stands out.

glossary.definition: Changing behaviour because we want acceptance or fear standing out.
glossary.example: Someone accepts a vape because they assume refusing will seem unfriendly.
glossary.limit: Pressure can exist without overt bullying or explicit orders.

glossary.definition: A pattern in which nicotine use is maintained partly by its effects and by withdrawal or craving.
glossary.example: Someone who initially tried vaping socially now feels uncomfortable when they go without it.
glossary.limit: Dependence requires attention to use over time; one social episode does not establish it.

glossary.definition: Making a decision that reflects your own reasons rather than untested expectations of others.
glossary.example: A student declines to vape and stays with the group to enjoy their company.
glossary.limit: Being included and using a particular product are not necessarily the same thing.
